title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is unauthorized data collection at the training stage. Suno admitted to training on what it described as essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the sources scraped. The outputs the system produces can reproduce recognizable elements of specific copyrighted recordings closely enough that plaintiffs were able to generate near-identical versions of named works using text prompts alone. This is a pre-deployment decision, made when the training corpus was assembled, with no licensing or rights-clearance step built in before that data was used.

The legal proceedings span multiple jurisdictions and plaintiffs. A German court ruled against Suno in a case brought by GEMA. Warner Music Group settled its lawsuit and entered a joint venture with Suno. Universal Music settled its lawsuit against Udio. A musicians' union then filed an amended lawsuit against Universal and Warner over those settlement deals. Record labels, independent artists, and a music publisher have all filed separate actions, and some cases remained active at the time of reporting.

What is not established is whether any court outside Germany has issued a final liability ruling on the core copyright infringement claims, whether Suno or Udio acted with the intent alleged in the lawsuits, or whether the dollar figures named in any complaint reflect what a court has awarded.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular artificial intelligence music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim the companies deliberately conceal which music they used for training, though both previously argued their use constitutes fair use under copyright law.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated their ability to recreate famous songs by inputting specific prompts into both AI systems and comparing the outputs to original recordings they own. Examples include generating versions resembling Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and nearly identical clones of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The labels submitted a comprehensive list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were scraped, featuring artists such as The Beatles, Michael Jackson, and Bruce Springsteen. The lawsuits, filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, also name unnamed individuals allegedly responsible for the music scraping and represent a significant legal battle regarding generative AI's use of copyrighted material.
